title: 5 things ADT monitoring agents want every Thanksgiving cook to know
summary: Thanksgiving is the busiest day of the year at ADT monitoring centers. The people who see what goes wrong share five ways to help keep holiday cooking on track.
body_markdown:
Thanksgiving is the[busiest day of the year for fire alarms](https://newsroom.adt.com/employee-experience/behind-the-scenes-of-a-safe-thanksgiving-adt-monitoring-has-your-back) at ADT monitoring centers. The people who know what can go wrong share five ways to help keep holiday cooking on track.


For many families, Thanksgiving means a full house and lots of food. That can lead to a busy kitchen, with multiple dishes in the oven, every burner in use, and distractions everywhere.


With so much cooking happening in homes across the country, Thanksgiving is the busiest day of the year for fire alarms at ADT monitoring centers. Last year, ADT received more than 10,900 fire alarms on Thanksgiving — 104% more than the day before.


“It’s constant waves of activity for us at ADT as Thanksgiving cooking moves across the different time zones,” says Ryan Mihalik, ADT Monitoring Unit Manager.


##### That front-row seat to Thanksgiving mishaps has taught the monitoring team a lot about what can go wrong in the kitchen. Here are five things ADT monitoring agents want cooks to keep in mind this year:


### 1. Stay close to what’s cooking


ADT monitoring agents have received fire alarms after customers stepped out of the house for a quick grocery run or became distracted by a phone call while something was on the stove. In one case, John Turner, ADT Senior Monitoring Unit Manager, recalled his team reaching a customer before the situation escalated.


“There was an alarm where a person fell asleep with the turkey in the oven, and we called and actually woke them up,” Turner said. “That’s the value of having your home professionally monitored, so even when you don’t realize something is wrong, we’re here and ready to respond.”


Monitoring agents recommend staying close to the kitchen, setting timers for individual dishes, and using more than one timer when several things are cooking at once. And if you need to leave the house, turn off the oven or stovetop rather than leave food cooking unattended.


> Our customers really value us because we’re their second set of eyes. They may be focused on cooking and celebrating with family, but we’re still paying attention.
>
>
> Latasha Campbell, ADT Monitoring Agent


### 2. Keep spills from becoming smoke


ADT monitoring agents have received alarms triggered by old grease and food burning inside ovens, as well as by turkey drippings, pans overflowing with broth, and other spills hitting hot surfaces and creating smoke.


Before cooking, monitoring agents recommend you check the oven for old spills that could create smoke as it heats up. Use roasting pans large enough to contain drippings and keep an eye on stovetop boil-overs, addressing them quickly rather than letting food or grease continue to burn on a hot surface.


### 3. Keep cooking surfaces clear


During Thanksgiving prep, crowded counters bring oven mitts, towels, paper towels and food packaging close to hot cooking surfaces. ADT monitoring agents have responded to fire alarms after items left on or near the stove caught on fire.


Before turning on the stove, agents suggest you do a quick check for anything flammable and move it away from the cooking area. Keep checking as you cook, especially as counters get crowded and more people start moving around the kitchen.


### 4. Think twice before you fry


“We know what can happen when a frozen turkey goes directly into extremely hot oil,” said Rhonda Thomas, ADT Monitoring Unit Manager. “You drop it in and boom! The oil can overflow, splatter or ignite. And within seconds, Thanksgiving dinner can turn into a fire that threatens your home.”


That’s why ADT monitoring agents stress fully thawing your turkey and patting it dry before frying. They also say follow the fryer’s instructions for the proper amount of oil. Set up the fryer outdoors on a flat, stable surface, avoid wooden decks, and keep the fryer well away from the home, garage and anything else that’s flammable.


### 5. Give the smoke somewhere to go


All that Thanksgiving cooking can create more smoke than people realize. ADT monitoring agents have heard from customers whose alarms continued sounding even after they stopped cooking because smoke was still lingering in the home. Their advice: Use your kitchen exhaust fan from the start and, if smoke begins to build and it’s safe to do so, open windows or use fans to help clear the air.


### One final thing NOT to do


ADT monitoring agents have heard from customers who disabled a smoke detector after cooking set it off. But disabling a detector can mean losing both the warning inside your home and the connection to ADT monitoring agents when you may need it most.


“Our customers really value us because we’re their second set of eyes,” said Latasha Campbell, ADT Monitoring Agent. “They may be focused on cooking and celebrating with family, but we’re still paying attention. If that alarm comes in, we’re going to receive it and respond quickly. We are always here for our customers when they need us”
